title: The nightly metrics job

story: It is December, and one of our engineering leaders asks the question this whole project exists to answer: since Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, started in October, do pull requests wait less for a review? You open the delivery dashboard. The review-wait line starts on 1 October, the night the metrics job (our program that turns GitHub history into weekly team numbers) first ran, and it has gone up and down since. Is the line high or low? Nobody can say, because there is nothing before Nova to compare it with.

You could have started the job in July, but it is too late for that now. The good news is that GitHub never forgot July: every pull request still has its timeline, with the minute it became ready for review and the minute each review arrived.
hook.question: How does a job that first runs in October write correct numbers for the weeks of July, August and September?

read.h: The past is still in GitHub
p: Three things are involved: GitHub, which keeps every pull request's history; the metrics job, a small TypeScript program that a GitHub Actions cron starts every night at 02:20; and VictoriaMetrics, the database our dashboards read. The job asks GitHub for a week of pull requests at a time, because GitHub's search returns at most 1000 results per query, and for each one it gets the commits and two kinds of timeline event: the moment a draft became ready for review, and every review with its author.

From that it computes review wait: the hours from "ready for review" (or from opening, if the PR was never a draft) to the first review by a person who is not the author. Each part of that sentence matters. Byte, our review agent, reviews every PR within minutes, and GitHub marks its reviews with the author type Bot. If Byte's review counted, review wait would drop to ten minutes the week Byte started, and the dashboard would celebrate a change nobody felt. A PR with no human review yet gives no number at all, not zero.

Notice that nothing in these functions depends on today's date. Review wait for a PR from July comes out exactly the same tonight as it would have on a night in July. That is what makes the rest of this lesson possible.

notes.text: The first ReadyForReviewEvent if the PR started as a draft, otherwise the moment it opened.
Bot reviews never count, and neither does the author reviewing their own PR.
undefined means "no human review yet". The caller leaves the PR out instead of counting it as 0 hours.
The Monday 00:00 UTC of the week a time falls in. A PR counts in the week it became ready for review.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the other numbers the job computes
p: Review wait is one of five delivery numbers that have history. Lead time runs from a PR's first commit to its merge. Change failure counts merged PRs that a revert, a hotfix or a Bug fix touched within 14 days. The share of PRs with AI help counts the "Co-Authored-By: Claude" trailer in commits or "Generated with Claude Code" in the PR body.

Red-main time is the hours main had a failing required unit-test job, read from the CI runs on main. Only the required unit-test jobs count, because the slower integration tests fail by chance now and then and would paint main red when the code is fine. If the cloud tests are red from 00:00 to 02:00 and the client tests from 01:00 to 03:00, main was red for 3 hours, not 4: the job walks the results in time order and counts the time when any job is red, once.

Every night the job also stores the raw answers from GitHub and Jira as a JSON file of the Actions run, so a mistake in a formula can be fixed and the numbers recomputed without asking the APIs again.

read.h: Stamp the week, not the night
p: A long-running service exposes counters and lets the database read them every few seconds, as you saw in the lesson about Prometheus metrics. A nightly job cannot work like that: it lives for two minutes and is gone. So it pushes its results to VictoriaMetrics' import endpoint as lines of Prometheus text, and it puts a timestamp at the end of each line, in milliseconds since 1970. The timestamp says which week the number is about, not when the job ran.

That single choice makes a backfill free. A backfill means computing numbers for past periods from history and writing them as if they had been written back then. The nightly run computes last week and stamps it with last week's Monday. The backfill runs the same code for each of the twelve weeks before October and stamps each with its own Monday. There is no second program to keep correct.
The values are finished numbers, a median per team and week, so a dashboard draws them as they are and never wraps them in rate(), which only makes sense for counters that keep growing.

code.file: what the job pushes (one line per team, week and number)
code.text:
delivery_review_wait_hours{team="frontend",q="p50"} 12.0 1788134400000
delivery_review_wait_hours{team="frontend",q="p85"} 17.6 1788134400000

# sent once, to the database's import endpoint:
node week.mjs | curl --data-binary @- http://<victoria-metrics>/api/v1/import/prometheus

notes.text: Name, labels, value, timestamp. 1788134400000 is Monday 31 August 2026, 00:00 UTC: the week this median describes.
p85 is the value 85 of 100 PRs stayed under. It shows the slow tail that a median hides.

read.see:
204
(204 means "accepted". It does not promise that every line was stored, as the lab shows.)

deeper.h: Go deeper: fixing a week you already wrote
p: If you push the same week again with a corrected value, VictoriaMetrics keeps both samples with the same timestamp, and you should not rely on which one a query returns. To correct the past, delete the series (the admin endpoint /api/v1/admin/tsdb/delete_series) and push the weeks again from the stored raw JSON. That is the reason the job keeps the raw answers: the fix is a recompute, not a patch on top.

Every time-series database keeps data for a limited time, called the retention period, and drops anything older. VictoriaMetrics' default is one month. That is fine for a service's live counters, but a backfill writes points from three months ago, and a database with the default setting rejects every one of them. The trap is how quietly it happens: the import still answers 204, the job reports success, and the only trace is a warning in the database's own log and a counter called vm_rows_ignored_total.

So before you trust a backfill, check two things: that the store keeps data for longer than the oldest week you write (our long-term store keeps it for years), and that the points are really there, by asking for them, not by reading the HTTP status.

read.h: Team numbers, a baseline, and no fake zeros
p: The job adds things up before it writes. Every series carries a team, which comes from the same email-to-team table the collector uses, and never a GitHub login. A team with fewer than 3 people is reported as "other", because a number about a team of two is really a number about two people. A median needs at least two PRs, so a quiet week writes no point for that team, and next to every median the job writes how many PRs it is based on, because weekly numbers for about 25 engineers jump around.

The backfill runs once, over the twelve weeks that end on 30 September, and its result is kept as separate series called delivery_baseline_*. That is the baseline: what normal looked like before any agent worked. In December, every delivery chart draws it as a flat reference line, which turns December's question into something you can answer by looking.

Numbers that only exist once agents work, such as how many agent PRs are merged, start as "no data" and not as 0. A chart that shows 0 for September and 60% for October tells a story of sudden improvement that never happened.

lab.title: Backfill three weeks of review wait
lab.goal: Compute review wait per team and week from pull-request history, push it with each week's own timestamp, and prove the points landed on the right weeks.

guess.q: It is October. You start VictoriaMetrics with its default settings and push three weeks of review wait from the start of September. curl prints 204. What does a query for those weeks return?

options.text: All three weeks, because 204 means the database accepted the data.
options.why: 204 means the request was fine. The database still checks each line and quietly skips the ones it will not keep.

options.text: Nothing: the default keeps one month, so points older than that are dropped, with a warning only in the database's log.
options.why: The default retention period is one month. Points older than that are counted in vm_rows_ignored_total and never stored.

options.text: The three points, but all placed on today's date, because the database stamps them on arrival.
options.why: The timestamp at the end of each line wins. Without one, the database would use the arrival time, which is exactly what a backfill must avoid.

check.q: The metrics job first ran on 1 October. How does the dashboard get review wait for August?

options.text: It cannot; history starts when the job starts
options.why: The job's input is GitHub's history, which still holds August. Only the output is new.

options.text: The backfill runs the same code over August's pull requests and stamps each number with its own week
options.why: Review wait depends only on each PR's timeline, so it comes out the same today. The timestamp puts it on the right week.

options.text: Grafana, the dashboard tool, estimates the missing weeks from the October trend
options.why: Grafana draws what is stored. It never invents past values, and a guess would be useless as a baseline.

check.q: Byte reviews every PR about ten minutes after it is ready. What happens to review wait if the job counts Byte's review as the first review?

options.text: Nothing; Byte is a reviewer like any other
options.why: Review wait measures how long a person waits for another person. A bot that answers in minutes measures nothing about that.

options.text: The job crashes, because bots have no login
options.why: Bots have logins. The danger is quieter: the numbers look plausible and are wrong.

options.text: It drops to about ten minutes for everyone, and the dashboard shows an improvement nobody felt
options.why: That is why the first review must come from an author of type User who is not the PR's author.

check.q: A team of two engineers merged five PRs last week. How does that week appear?

options.text: Under team="other", together with every team under 3 people
options.why: A number about a team of two is a number about two people. Folding small teams into "other" keeps every number at team level.

options.text: Under the team's own name, because five PRs are enough for a median
options.why: The number of PRs decides whether a median exists. The size of the team decides whether it may be shown under its name.

options.text: Under each engineer's GitHub login, so the numbers are more precise
options.why: No series ever carries a login. That rule holds for every number in the job.

p: The job lives in the ai-agents repo as the metrics workspace, TypeScript on Node 24: src/github.ts pulls fcp PRs with one GraphQL query per week (searched once by created date and once by merged date), src/jira.ts pulls RH tickets updated in the last 13 weeks with a read-only Jira account, src/ci.ts reads the required unit-test jobs of cloud-ci.yml, client-ci.yml and frontend-ci.yaml on main, and src/compute.ts turns it all into weekly team points. The command is delivery-metrics, with nightly and backfill --weeks 12.

It runs from .github/workflows/delivery-metrics.yml on cron '20 2 * * *'. GitHub is read with a separate read-only GitHub App, so the rhino-ai-agents key stays with the broker alone. Points are pushed to the integration VMUser the same way infrastructure's send-workflow-result.yml does it, with the password read from Secrets Manager through the GitHubActions OIDC role. The baseline comes from delivery-metrics backfill --weeks 12 --until 2026-09-30, checked by hand against GitHub for three numbers, and stored as delivery_baseline_*. Byte's rates and the runtime's run numbers are copied into the same delivery_* names, so one dashboard holds all of them.

tickets.why: The metrics workspace, the GitHub query one week at a time, the push with timestamps and the nightly workflow.
Jira tickets and red-main time from the required unit-test jobs, plus the raw JSON kept for recomputing.
The delivery formulas, teams and cohorts, "no data" instead of 0, and the 12-week backfill that becomes the baseline.

words.plain: Hours from "ready for review" to the first review by a person who is not the author. Bot reviews do not count.
Computing numbers for past periods from history and writing them with the past period's timestamp.
What normal looked like before a change: here, the 12 weeks before October.
How long a database keeps data. Points older than it are dropped, also when you write them.
The value that 85 out of 100 items stay under. It shows the slow tail that a median hides.

review.q: Write the rule for review wait in one sentence, with both of its exceptions.
review.a: From ready for review (or opening, if never a draft) to the first review by a User who is not the author; bot reviews do not count, and a PR with no human review gives no number instead of 0.

review.q: A backfill answered 204 but the dashboard is empty for those weeks. What do you check first?
review.a: The database's retention period and its ignored-rows counter (vm_rows_ignored_total with reason small_timestamp), then query the weeks directly.

review.q: Why do numbers that only exist with agents start as "no data" and not 0?
review.a: A 0 before October and a real value after it draws a sudden improvement that never happened; no data draws nothing.

remember: Compute from history and stamp each number with the week it describes, so the backfill and the nightly run are the same code, and check that the past really landed.
